# SMTP Connect() failed. Message was not sent

When you encounter an `SMTP -> ERROR: Failed to connect to server: Connection timed out (110)` error, the immediate assumption is often that your network connection is down or the remote server is unreachable. While those are valid possibilities, in the context of Gmail and PHPMailer, the culprit is almost always a mismatch between your configuration and Google's current security requirements.

The code snippet provided attempts to connect to `smtp.gmail.com` on port 587 using SSL (`ssl://smtp.gmail.com`). This syntax is technically incorrect for the intended protocol. Port 587 is designated for SMTP over TLS (Transport Layer Security), not SSL. When you prepend `ssl://` to the hostname, you are attempting to initiate an SSL handshake on a port that expects a plain text SMTP conversation or a STARTTLS command first. This protocol mismatch frequently results in connection timeouts because the server rejects the initial greeting or cannot negotiate the secure channel as requested.

To resolve this, you must align your configuration with the specific transport layer security required by the host:

```php
$mail->IsSMTP();
$mail->Host = 'smtp.gmail.com'; // Remove 'ssl://' prefix for port 587
$mail->Port = 587;              // Standard submission port
$mail->SMTPSecure = 'tls';      // Explicitly define TLS encryption
$mail->SMTPAuth = true;
$mail->Username = "myemail@gmail.com";
$mail->Password = "mypassword";
```

However, fixing the connection string is only half the battle. Gmail enforces strict authentication policies that often trip up legacy PHPMailer setups. If your application runs on a shared host or a local server without valid TLS certificates, connecting to `smtp.gmail.com` over port 465 (which uses implicit SSL) might also fail due to certificate validation issues, though port 587 with STARTTLS is the modern standard.

A critical pitfall in the provided code is the handling of credentials. Storing plain-text passwords directly in the source code (`Password = "mypasswword"`) is a significant security vulnerability. If you are deploying this to a production environment, you must use environment variables or a secure credential vault. Furthermore, Gmail recently deprecated support for third-party applications using standard application passwords if 2-Factor Authentication (2FA) is enabled on the account.

If you have 2FA enabled, you cannot simply paste your regular login password into the `$mail->Password` property. You must generate an "App Password" specifically for mail access within your Google Account settings and use that value in the script. Failing to do this will result in authentication errors even after fixing the connection timeout.

Another potential issue lies in the `SetFrom()` method. The code shows `$mail->SetFrom($visitor_email, $name);`. If `$visitor_email` is an address not verified as belonging to you (i.e., it's not your own Gmail account or a domain you control), Gmail will likely reject the message due to spoofing protections. You should verify that the sender address matches the authenticated username or is a verified alias for your domain.

For developers working within the Laravel ecosystem, this manual configuration of PHPMailer is often unnecessary and prone to these exact errors. The `laravel/framework` package includes a robust `Mail` facade that abstracts SMTP handling, automatically managing connection timeouts, retries, and TLS negotiation. If you are maintaining an older codebase relying on raw PHPMailer, consider refactoring to the Laravel mail driver or ensuring your custom configuration strictly adheres to the TLS requirements outlined above.

If you require a deeper dive into configuring email services within modern PHP frameworks, including best practices for handling SMTP credentials securely and setting up transport drivers, you might find the resources available at [https://laravelcompany.com](https://laravelcompany.com) helpful for integrating these solutions into your workflow.
